title: Allee effect

definition.text: The link between how many individuals a population has, or how dense it is, and how well the average individual survives and reproduces; at low numbers, fewer individuals means lower fitness.

facts.text: It is usually defined as positive density dependence: individual fitness rises with population density.
The classical view held that competition makes growth fastest at low density; the Allee effect says the reverse at low density.
Warder Clyde Allee first described it in the 1930s, showing goldfish survive better in tanks with more fish.
Common causes are trouble finding mates, cooperative defence, cooperative feeding and environmental conditioning.
In fisheries science it is close to, or the same as, 'depensation'.
It can slow a population's range expansion and even prevent biological invasions.
Fishing pressure combined with Allee effects can push exploited fish populations between alternative stable states.

contested_note: Sources call it contentious whether demographic stochasticity counts as an Allee effect.

title: Strong and weak Allee effects
article: Allee effect#Strong vs. weak Allee effects

definition.text: Two kinds of Allee effect, distinguished by whether the population has a critical size below which its growth turns negative.

facts.text: Under a weak Allee effect, growth per individual slows at low numbers but stays positive.
Under a strong Allee effect, a population that falls below the threshold is headed for extinction without help.
A simple cubic growth model shows this: growth is negative between zero and a threshold A and positive between A and carrying capacity K.

definition.text: An Allee effect created by markets, when rarity makes a species so valuable that hunting the last individuals still pays.

facts.text: Classic economic theory expected exploitation to stop short of extinction, because the cost of finding the last few individuals would exceed their selling price.
When rare species fetch higher prices than common ones, rare species can be driven extinct while common ones are harvested sustainably.
It is now a standard way to think about how markets threaten endangered species.
A two-dimensional analysis shows even very large populations can be on paths to extinction.

definition.text: The movement of living things, or their seeds and spores, from where they were born to where they breed, or from one breeding site to another.

facts.text: Technically it is any movement that could lead to gene flow.
It has three phases: departure, transfer and settlement.
Organisms disperse when the benefits, such as new resources and avoiding competition and inbreeding, outweigh the costs in energy, risk, time and opportunity.
Dispersal shapes population dynamics, population genetics and where species live.
Ecosystems depend on individuals moving between habitat patches, making dispersal critical to their stability.
Seed dispersal and the ability to disperse are counted as ecosystem services and as part of a species' capacity to adapt to climate change.

definition.text: The movement of seeds away from the parent plant.

facts.text: The five main modes are gravity, wind, ballistic, water and animals.
How seeds disperse shapes the genetic structure, migration and species interactions of plant populations.
Transport by animals is especially effective because it carries seeds over long distances.
Because plants cannot move much, they rely on wind and water or on animals such as birds and mammals to carry their seeds.

definition.text: Anything that stops organisms from moving, so that a species' dispersal range is smaller than its distribution.

facts.text: Habitat fragmentation from human land use is an artificial barrier; mountain ranges and rivers are natural ones.
The Congo River separates the ranges of the two chimpanzee species.
Barriers that cut gene flow can isolate populations and lead to allopatric speciation.

definition.text: A probability distribution describing how far individuals travel when they disperse.

facts.text: Dispersal is measured either as a rate, the expected share of individuals leaving an area, or as a distance.
Models use kernels such as the negative exponential, normal and inverse power distributions.
'Fat-tailed' kernels that allow rare long-distance moves are thought to fit real data best.

definition.text: Movement of organisms that people cause, either by carrying them directly or by altering landscapes.

facts.text: People move organisms on purpose, as with farm animals, or by accident when they cling to people or vehicles.
Carriage by humans can move organisms much farther than natural means.
Ship ballast water and motor vehicles are new dispersal routes that can spread invasive species.

definition.text: A simple mathematical model of how the populations of species competing for a shared resource change over time.

facts.text: It builds on the logistic equation, adding for each species a term for the harm done by its competitors.
For two species, the coefficient α12 is the effect of species 2 on species 1 and α21 the reverse; in competition all these values are positive.
Each species can have its own growth rate and carrying capacity.
The model extends to any number of species, with the interaction coefficients forming a matrix.
Competitive systems cannot cycle with fewer than three species or become chaotic with fewer than four; with five or more, any behaviour is possible.
Large Lotka–Volterra systems tend to be unstable or sparsely connected, unless species' traits evolve by natural selection.

definition.text: A discrete-time model of population growth that tracks a population divided into age classes.

facts.text: It assumes a population closed to migration, growing without limits, and usually counts only females.
Building it requires the count in each age class, the share surviving to the next class, and fecundity for each class.
Each time step, the population vector is multiplied by the matrix to give the next step's population.
The matrix's dominant eigenvalue gives the long-run growth rate, and its eigenvector gives the stable age distribution.

definition.text: The steady share of individuals in each age class that an age-structured population settles into, along with a steady growth rate.

facts.text: Whatever its starting size or age mix, the population tends toward this structure, and returns to it after disturbance.
Once reached, the population grows exponentially at rate λ.
Fast-growing populations, and those with high death rates at all ages, have disproportionately young age structures.

title: Diffusion of innovations S-curve
article: Logistic function#In economics and sociology: diffusion of innovations

definition.text: Use of the logistic curve to show how an innovation spreads: slowly at first, then rapidly, then levelling off near saturation.

facts.text: Gabriel Tarde's The Laws of Imitation (1890) described three stages: a hard start, an exponential take-off, and a slowing phase.
New products such as railroads, light bulbs, electrification, cars and air travel went through rapid growth after early cost and quality gains.

definition.text: A pair of differential equations, also called the predator–prey model, that describe how the numbers of a predator and its prey change together over time.

facts.text: Prey grow exponentially without predators, and are eaten at a rate proportional to how often predators and prey meet.
Predators grow by eating prey and, without prey, die off exponentially.
The model predicts endless cycles: predators thrive on plentiful prey, outstrip their food and decline, letting prey recover.
Such swings are seen in nature, as in Hudson's Bay Company lynx and snowshoe hare records and Isle Royale's moose and wolves.
Improving conditions for the prey raises the predator's equilibrium numbers, not the prey's.
Ocean iron fertilization fits this: the phytoplankton bloom is quickly eaten, so enrichment mainly boosts predators.
Lotka proposed the model in 1910 and Volterra published it independently in 1926 to explain why predatory fish rose in Adriatic catches during World War I.
In economics it models competing firms and, through Richard Goodwin's model, the link between unemployment and wage growth.

title: Minimum viable population

definition.text: The smallest size at which a population can survive in the wild without being wiped out by disasters or by random demographic, environmental or genetic events.

facts.text: Small populations face more extinction risk because they recover less well from random events.
It is estimated with population viability analyses, computer simulations repeated thousands of times to find the starting size giving, say, a 95% or 99% chance of surviving 1,000 years.
In small populations, genetic drift erodes genetic diversity and raises inbreeding, which lowers fitness.
The '50/500 rule' is a common benchmark, but 2014 guidance says it does not apply across many taxa.
A meta-analysis found a median MVP for vertebrates of 4,169 individuals (95% CI = 3,577–5,129).
Managers can lift a population above its MVP through captive breeding or by moving in individuals from other reserves.

contested_note: Sources note debate over how accurate population viability analyses are, since forecasts need many assumptions.

definition.text: The mathematical study of how the size and age make-up of populations change over time, treating them as dynamical systems.

facts.text: It is a branch of mathematical biology that uses tools such as differential equations.
It is widely seen as beginning with Malthus, who held that with constant conditions a population grows or declines exponentially.
Simple models track four processes: births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
In a closed population, growth equals births minus deaths: dN/dt = rN.
Adding a carrying capacity gives the logistic equation, in which growth is limited as N approaches K.
Population ecologists use life-history data and projection matrices to manage wildlife stocks and set harvest quotas.

definition.text: The rate at which a population would grow, per individual, if nothing dependent on its density held it back.

facts.text: It is the r in dN/dt = rN, the maximum theoretical growth rate per individual.
It is often used in insect pest management to see how the environment affects how fast pests multiply.
It relates to the finite rate of increase λ of generation-based models by r = ln(λ).

definition.text: Growth of a population that breeds in separate seasons, multiplying by a fixed factor λ each generation.

facts.text: With constant birth and death rates, the population after t generations is λ^t times its starting size.
It grows if births exceed deaths (λ > 1), shrinks if deaths exceed births, and holds steady if they are equal.
Doubling time is the time for the population to reach twice its size, found by taking logarithms.
Real populations cannot grow forever, because lack of resources eventually raises the death rate.

title: R/K selection theory

definition.text: An evolutionary hypothesis that species are selected either to produce many cheap offspring or few offspring with heavy parental investment.

facts.text: r-strategists have many offspring with little care each; K-strategists invest heavily in fewer offspring.
The letters come from the logistic model: r is the maximum growth rate and K the carrying capacity.
r-selection dominates in unstable environments and favours many offspring, small size, early maturity and wide dispersal; dandelions are a typical example.
K-selection dominates in stable environments, favouring strong competitors with large bodies, long lives and few well-cared-for young, such as elephants and whales.
Most organisms mix traits; the split can be recast with discounting, r-selection matching large discount rates and K-selection small ones.
MacArthur and Wilson coined the terms in 1967; the theory was popular in the 1970s and 1980s, then lost ground after empirical criticism.
Life history theory based on age-specific mortality has replaced it, and some now speak of fast versus slow life histories.
Slow-breeding, long-lived species such as orange roughy proved vulnerable to fishing models that assumed faster growth.

contested_note: Empirical studies from 1977 to 1994 contradicted its predictions, and reviewers judged it a once-useful heuristic that life history theory has superseded.

definition.text: The pattern in which fast-breeding r-strategists colonize disturbed land first and are gradually replaced by more competitive K-strategists.

facts.text: After major disruptions such as the eruptions at Krakatoa or Mount St. Helens, the two strategies play distinct roles in regrowth.
Succession approaches a new equilibrium, sometimes called a climax community, dominated by K-strategists.
The intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds that moderate disturbance creates patches at different stages, letting colonizers and competitors coexist.

definition.text: In population dynamics, the process by which new individuals join a population, through birth and growing up or through immigration.

facts.text: An individual often counts as recruited only once it survives to a certain size or life stage.
It is shaped by predation, birth and dispersal rates and by temperature, rainfall and disturbance, which makes it hard to measure.
High recruitment raises current and future abundance; low recruitment reduces it.
Because of their economic importance, fisheries are a common setting for recruitment studies; fishing a stock at or below MSY keeps it at maximum recruitment.

title: Species–area relationship

definition.text: The pattern linking the area of a habitat to the number of species found in it: larger areas tend to hold more species.

facts.text: It is often fitted with Preston's power function, which plots as a straight line on log–log axes with slope z.
Plotted on ordinary axes the curve almost always flattens as area grows.
Proposed causes include the balance of immigration and extinction, disturbance, predator–prey dynamics and clustering of individuals.
Conservation scientists use it to predict extinction rates from habitat loss and fragmentation.
Preston distinguished 'mainland' samples of continuous habitat from 'island' isolates such as islands.
Island biogeography theory was first developed to explain the species–area pattern on oceanic islands.
It is often written as the power law S = cA^z, where S is species number, A is area and z the slope.
On log–log axes it becomes a straight line: log(S) = log(c) + z log(A).

notes: S:bab7f90e94a7: a 2006 meta-analysis found island slopes lower than mainland ones, contrary to earlier presumption.

definition.text: Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals owing to differences in their relative fitness.

facts.text: It is a key mechanism of evolution that changes the heritable traits of a population or species over generations.
It needs heritable variation that raises lifetime reproductive rate; if such variation is passed from parent to offspring, reproduction becomes differential.
Darwin set out the theory in 1859 to explain adaptation and speciation: individuals best adapted to their environments are more likely to survive and reproduce.
Selection is not always directional or adaptive; it often maintains the status quo by eliminating less fit variants.
Misuse of antibiotics has selected for resistant microbes, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), called a superbug.
Integration with Mendel's laws in the early 20th-century modern synthesis led scientists to accept natural selection, which remains the foundation of evolutionary theory.

definition.text: In modern evolutionary theory, fitness is how successful an organism is at reproducing, not how long it lives.

facts.text: The concept is central to natural selection; 'survival of the fittest' hides a much subtler meaning.
Traits that raise reproductive success are selected for; those that lower it are selected against.

definition.text: Selection can be classified by its effect on a trait, on genetic diversity, by life cycle stage, by unit of selection, or by resource competed for.

facts.text: Stabilizing selection holds a trait at an optimum, while directional selection favours extreme values.
Purifying selection removes genetic variation; balancing selection maintains it through negative frequency-dependent selection.
Viability selection raises survival probability; fecundity selection raises reproductive rate.
Sexual selection is competition for mates and typically proceeds via fecundity selection, sometimes at the expense of viability.

definition.text: Gene flow, also called migration, is the transfer of genetic material from one population to another.

facts.text: If its rate is high enough two populations share equivalent allele frequencies and count as one effective population; one migrant per generation is enough to prevent drift-driven divergence.
High gene flow reduces genetic differentiation and can constrain speciation and range expansion, though it can also add novel variants under positive selection (adaptive introgression).
It is estimated directly from dispersal and reproductive success, or indirectly by comparing allele frequencies; with one migrant per generation FST equals 0.2.
Barriers can be physical, as in allopatric speciation, or reproductive, as in sympatric speciation; the Great Wall of China has hindered gene flow in native plants.
Hybridization with introduced species can swamp a rare species' gene pool; introgression is replacement of one species' alleles with an invader's.
Its effects are context-dependent: it can enhance a population's fitness or have negative consequences.

definition.text: Assisted gene flow is a management strategy that conserves at-risk species by simulating natural gene flow, moving individuals or gametes between populations.

facts.text: Moving individuals within a species' existing range can help it adapt to projected local climate conditions.
It can introduce pre-adapted genotypes or raise the frequency of existing climate-adapted ones, and suits any species whose habitat will change greatly.

definition.text: Two models describe how urbanization affects gene flow: habitat fragmentation, which lowers genetic diversity, and urban facilitation, which connects populations.

facts.text: Urban facilitation reduces isolation and brings previously separated species into contact, directly or indirectly.
Whether corridors work depends on species' dispersal abilities and adaptiveness to anthropogenic structures.

title: Genetic drift

definition.text: Genetic drift is the change in the frequency of an existing allele in a population due to chance.

facts.text: Drift can remove alleles completely, cutting genetic variation, or push a rare allele to fixation where it displaces all others.
Random sampling can remove but not replace an allele, so drift drives a population toward genetic uniformity; an allele at frequency 1 is fixed and at 0 is lost.
With drift alone, an allele's chance of eventual fixation equals its frequency, and fixation comes much faster in smaller populations.
The effective population size, smaller than the total population, is used for these calculations.
Selection has a direction toward adaptation; drift has none and acts on genotype frequencies regardless of phenotypic effect. Both act together with mutation and migration.
Fisher thought drift played at most a minor role; Kimura's 1968 neutral theory claimed most spread of genetic change comes from drift acting on neutral mutations.

contested_note: Biologists have debated since the mid 20th century how much evolution is driven by drift versus natural selection.

definition.text: A population bottleneck is a sharp contraction in population size over a short time due to a random environmental event.

facts.text: Survival in a true bottleneck is random, not improved by any genetic advantage, so allele frequencies can change radically independent of selection and inbreeding increases afterward.
The founder effect is a special case: a small group splits off and forms a new population whose alleles grossly misrepresent the original population.
Founder effects can shape a small colony's genetics far into the future, as with the recessive Ellis-Van Creveld allele in the 1744 Amish migration to Pennsylvania.

title: Intermediate disturbance hypothesis

definition.text: The intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds that local species diversity is highest when ecological disturbance is neither too rare nor too frequent.

facts.text: At low disturbance, competitive species push others to extinction; at high disturbance, all species risk extinction.
At intermediate levels, species of early and late successional stages coexist, because moderate disturbance prevents interspecific competition from running to exclusion.
K-selected species dominate stable ecosystems; r-selected species colonize recently cleared areas; occasional disturbance lets both live together.
It is a nonequilibrium model, with Connell usually cited as its founder, and the hump-backed graph shows diversity against disturbance.

The hypothesis is ambiguous about what counts as intermediate or as disturbance, which depends on the system's disturbance history and on whether frequency, extent, intensity or duration is evaluated.

contested_note: The terms intermediate and disturbance are ambiguous, and the marine Menge-Sutherland model showed a discrepancy with it.

definition.text: Life history theory is a framework for studying the diversity of life history strategies and the causes and results of variation in organisms' life cycles.

facts.text: A life history strategy is the age- and stage-specific pattern and timing of events such as maturation, reproduction and death, shaped by the organism's physical and ecological environment.
The theory arose in the 1950s and addresses questions of body size, age of maturation, number of offspring and life span.
Fitness is often assessed as the number of descendants over a lifetime, mainly survivorship and reproductive rate.
Environments in which resources, hazards and competitors fluctuate rapidly select for earlier reproduction and more offspring.
High mortality rates, the usual result of an unpredictable environment, typically go with earlier maturity than low mortality rates.
r/K selection theory frames the central trade-off, number of offspring against timing of reproduction.

definition.text: Life history trade-offs arise because an organism has limited energy and must choose among growth, reproduction and survival.

facts.text: Examples are the trade-off between maximizing body size and lifespan, and between offspring size and number.
Trade-offs limit adaptation and fitness; without them a hypothetical Darwinian demon would have the highest fitness.
Populations can reach an optimal strategy that maximizes fitness, which depends on how resources are allocated.

title: Capital and income breeding
article: Life history theory#Capital and income breeding

definition.text: Capital and income breeding describe how organisms finance and time breeding with resources.

facts.text: Capital breeders pay for breeding with resources gathered earlier and breed once body condition passes a threshold; income breeders use resources generated during breeding.
The two form a spectrum rather than a strict dichotomy.

definition.text: The paradox of enrichment is the idea that increasing the food available to a prey species can destabilize the predator's population.

facts.text: Michael Rosenzweig coined it in 1971; enrichment was modelled as higher prey carrying capacity, which can make the equilibrium unstable, usually giving a limit cycle.
The predator boom can crash and may lead to local eradication or extinction of the predator.
Past a critical carrying capacity the system undergoes a Hopf bifurcation; the result is counterintuitive, hence 'paradox'.
Empirical support comes mainly from small laboratory experiments, with limited field support.

Destabilisation need not occur with inedible, invulnerable or unpalatable prey, a ratio-dependent functional response such as the Arditi-Ginzburg model, spatial heterogeneity, inducible defense, or density-dependent predator mortality.

definition.text: A population pyramid is a graph of a population's distribution by age group and sex, usually for a country or region.

facts.text: Males are conventionally on the left and females on the right, with bars in absolute numbers or percentages.
In ecology it shows a population's age distribution, hinting at reproductive capability and likelihood of continuation.
A broad base signals fertility above replacement; the shape also reveals the age-dependency ratio of those too young or old to work.
Pyramids fall into three types: stationary, with births and deaths roughly balanced; expansive, wide at young ages; and constrictive, narrowed at the bottom.
Their shape tracks the demographic transition: more developed countries sit in stages three to five, least developed in stages one and two.

title: Youth bulge

definition.text: A youth bulge is a type of expansive population pyramid with a large share of young people.

facts.text: Large cohorts entering the labor force strain economy and polity, creating unemployment unless opportunities arise fast enough; then a demographic dividend accrues as workers outweigh dependents.

In developing countries youth bulges go with higher unemployment and a heightened risk of violence and instability; a 2016 study found they raise the chance of non-ethnic civil wars but not ethnic ones.
Suggested policy responses include creating jobs, improving family planning and reducing infant mortality.
In the Middle East and North Africa about 65% of the population is under 25; the region's youth bulge has been called a demographic gift that could fuel growth if harnessed.

notes: Heinsohn's unrest claims are contested in the source; stated only as the cited 2016 study and policy facts.

title: Population viability analysis

definition.text: Population viability analysis is a species-specific risk assessment method in conservation biology that gives the probability a population goes extinct within a set number of years.

facts.text: It combines species characteristics and environmental variability to forecast population health and extinction risk, with each analysis built for one target population.
It is used to judge urgency of recovery, find key life stages, compare management options, and assess impacts of habitat loss.
Mark Shaffer's 1978 grizzly bear model at Yellowstone calculated extinction probabilities and minimum viable population size; US use grew with the Endangered Species Act of 1973.

A PVA of Fender's blue butterfly found it more at risk than thought and located key recovery sites; one of the Santa Catalina island fox found it highly susceptible to catastrophes more often than once every 20 years.
Critics note precise forecasts T years ahead may need five to ten times T years of data, and suitable data exist for only 2% of threatened birds.
Retrospective tests show projections are accurate with sound or long-term data; its value lies more in assessing threats than making long-term categorical predictions.

contested_note: Debates remain unresolved over appropriate uses of PVA and its ability to assess extinction risk accurately.
